english:
I have no need to explain what a *dream* is. As for the *vision* (מראה), — for example, *I make myself known unto him in a vision* (Numbers, 12:6), — which is designated by the name of מראֵה הנבואה, *prophetic vision*[^2], which (in Scripture) is also called יד י״י, *hand of the Eternal*[^3], and which also bears the name of M<small>A</small>’<small>HAZÉ</small> (מחזה) [^4], it is a state of agitation and terror which seizes the prophet when he is awake, as is set forth, concerning Daniel, in these words: *I saw this great vision, and there remained no strength in me; for my comeliness was turned in me into corruption, and I retained no strength;* and he continues: *I fell stunned upon my face, having my face toward the ground* (Daniel, 10:8, 9). When afterwards the angel addresses him and causes him to stand, this still takes place within the *prophetic vision*. In such a state, the senses cease to function; that emanation (of which I have spoken) spreads over the rational faculty, and thence over the imaginative faculty, so that the latter is perfected and functions[^1]. Sometimes the revelation begins with a prophetic vision; then this agitation and this strong emotion, a consequence of the perfect action of the imagination, go on increasing, and then the (true) revelation arrives. This is what took place for Abraham; for (in speaking) of this revelation, one begins by saying: *The word of the Eternal came unto Abram in a vision* (Genesis, 15:1), and at the end (it is said), *and a deep sleep fell upon Abram* (ibid., v. 12); and afterwards: *And he said unto Abram etc.* (ibid., v. 13-16).

[^2]: The author means that what Scripture calls מראׇה, the theologians explain by מראֵה הנבואה, *that which is seen in the state of prophecy, prophetic vision*.
[^3]: See 2 Kings, 3:15; Ezekiel, 1:3; III, 22; XXXVII, 1; XL, 1.
[^4]: Word derived from the verb ’<small>HAZA</small> (הזה), *to see*. See Genesis, 15:1; Numbers, 24:4 and 16.
[^1]: See above, at the beginning of chap. XXXVII.
tr_notes: The citation 'III, 22' in footnote 3 refers to the book of Ezekiel mentioned previously in the list.
The term 'épanchement' is rendered as 'emanation' to reflect the philosophical context of the Arabic 'fayd'.

english:
Know that those among the prophets who recount having had a revelation, sometimes attribute it (expressly) to an angel, sometimes to God, although it undoubtedly took place through the mediation of an angel; the doctors have pronounced upon this, saying: “*And the Eternal said unto her* (ibid., XXV, 23), through the mediation of an angel[^2].” — It must be known that, whenever a passage (of Scripture) says of someone that an angel spoke to him, or that the word of God was addressed to him, this could not have taken place otherwise than in a dream or in a prophetic vision.

[^2]: See *Beréschîth rabbâ*, sect. 63 (fol. 55, col. 2), where R. Levi says, in the name of R. Aba, that God spoke to Rebecca through the mediation of an angel.

The terms employed in the prophetic books present to us four modes of expressing the word addressed to the prophets[^3]: The first mode, (is when) the prophet says expressly[^4] that this discourse came from the *angel*, in a *dream* or in a *vision*. The second mode is that he reports only the discourse which was addressed to him by the *angel*, without saying expressly that it was in a dream, or in a vision, being certain that it is a thing (generally) known that no revelation exists except in one of the two ways: *I make myself known unto him in a vision, I speak unto him in a dream* (Numbers, 12:6). The third mode is that he speaks not at all of an angel, but attributes the word to *God*, who would have addressed it to him Himself, declaring however that this word reached him in a *vision* or in a *dream*. The fourth mode is that the prophet says simply that *God* spoke to him, or that He commanded him to act[^1], to do (such a thing) or to speak in such a manner, without his speaking expressly either of an angel or of a dream, relying on what is known and has been established as a principle[^2], (namely) that no prophecy, no revelation, arrives otherwise than in a dream, or in a vision, and through the mediation of an angel.

[^3]: Literally: *The relation* (or *the statement*) *of the word addressed to the prophets, according to the expression which presents itself in the prophetic books, is made in four ways*.
[^4]: In none of our mss. is the verb יצרח preceded by the conjunction אן; and likewise, Ibn-Tibbon has simply יגله. The version of Al-’Harîzi bears שיאמר הנביא.
[^1]: The two Hebrew translators have omitted the imperative אפعل, because of its synonymy with אצנע.
[^2]: In the version of Ibn-Tibbon, even in the mss., we read והשודש, which is evidently a copyist's error for והושרש.

One expresses oneself according to the first mode in the following passages: *And the angel of God spake unto me in a dream* (Genesis, 31:11); *And God spake unto Israel in the visions of the night* (ibid., XLVI, 2); *And God came unto Balaam; And God said unto Balaam* (Numbers, 22:9 and 12)[^3]. — For the second mode, one may cite the following examples: *And God said unto Jacob: Arise, go up to Bethel* (Genesis, 35:1); *And God said unto him: thy name is Jacob* (ibid., v. 10); *And an angel of the Eternal called unto him out of heaven; And the angel of the Eternal called unto him a second time etc.* (ibid., XXII, 11 and 15); *And God said unto Noah* (ibid., VI, 13); *And God spake unto Noah* (ibid., VIII, 15). — An example of the third mode is found in this passage: *The word of the Eternal came unto Abram in a vision etc.* (ibid., XV, 1). — For the fourth mode, one finds the following examples: *And the Eternal said unto Abram* (ibid., XII, 1); *The Eternal said unto Jacob: Return into the land of thy fathers* (ibid., XXXI, 3); *And the Eternal said unto Joshua* (Joshua, 3:7); *And the Eternal said unto Gideon* (Judges, 7:2)[^1]. And it is thus that they (the prophets) express themselves for the most part: *And the Eternal said unto me* (Isaiah, 8:1); *And the word of the Eternal came unto me* (Ezekiel, XXIV, 1); *And the word of the Eternal came* (2 Samuel, 24:11; 1 Kings, XVIII, 1); *And behold, the word of the Eternal came to him* (1 Kings, 19:9)[^2]; *The word of the Eternal came* (Ezekiel, 1:3); *The beginning of the word of the Eternal by Hosea* (Hosea, I, 2); *The hand of the Eternal was upon me* (Ezekiel, 37:1; XL, 1). There are many examples of this kind.

[^3]: In the last three examples, as in those of the second mode, the word <small>ÉLOHIM</small> (God) designates, according to our author, an *angel* (see Vol. I, ch. II, p. 37, and above, ch. VI, p. 66), and it is to be remarked that, for the third and fourth mode, the author cites only examples where God is designated by the *tetragrammaton* name. Concerning the last two examples, it must be remembered that, if it is not expressly said there that the vision of Bileam took place in a dream, this results from verse 8, where Bileam says to the ambassadors of Balak: *Lodge here this night, and I will bring you word again*. — The second and third examples are missing in the version of Ibn-Tibbon.
[^1]: If the author cites here the example of Gideon, it must be understood in the sense that the word of the Eternal was addressed to a prophet who spoke to Gideon; for Gideon himself was not a prophet, as the author declares further on, chap. XLVI.
[^2]: The words והנה דבר י״י אליו are also found in chap. XV of Genesis, verse 4; but the author could not have had this passage in view, which is connected with verse 1 of the same chapter, and belongs, consequently, to the third mode.

All that is presented according to one of these four modes is a prophecy, and he who utters it is a prophet. But, when it is said: “God *came* unto such a one in a *dream* of the night,” it is not at all a matter of prophecy, and that person is not a prophet. In effect, it is meant (only) that there came to this person a warning on the part of God, and we are then told that this warning was made by means of a dream; for, just as God causes such a person to set himself in motion to save another person or to destroy him, so He causes to arise, by means of what is seen in a dream, certain things which He wishes to bring about. Certainly, we do not doubt that Laban the Aramean was a perfect villain and at the same time an idolater; and, as for Abimelech, although in the midst of his people he was a pious man, our father Abraham said of his city and of his kingdom: *Surely the fear of God is not in this place* (Genesis, 20:11); and yet, of each of the two, I mean of Laban and of Abimelech, it is said (that God appeared to him in a dream): *And God came to Abimelech in
